title: Sanada Yukimura Never Went by "Yukimura"? 4 Letters in His Hand, None Signed That Name
description:
In Taishō 6 (1917), Tokyo Imperial University's Dai Nihon Shiryō, Part 12, Volume 19, printed a plate titled "Letter of Sanada Yukimura"; yet the signature at the letter's end reads "Saemon-no-suke Nobushige," preceded by the first character of Sanada. Did he ever call himself "Yukimura"?

The letters he wrote inside Osaka Castle are signed Nobushige or Saemon-no-suke; a letter from his Kudoyama years asking for shōchū is signed "Kōhaku, Nobushige." He died in battle at Osaka on Keichō 20, 5th month, 7th day (June 3, 1615, Gregorian). The enemy daimyo Hosokawa Tadaoki, in a letter of the 5th month, 15th day, calls him "Sanada Saemon-no-suke"; a postwar report kept by the Shimazu clan (writer unknown) relays "Sanada, the finest warrior in Japan," but names him only "Sanada Saemon" and "Sanada"; the "Yukimura" beside it is a small later addition. The first book to write "Yukimura" is generally thought to be the Naniwa Senki (preface dated 1672; we read an undated expanded version, further rewritten in 1928). In the Tōgen Iji, compiled after Tokugawa Mitsukuni died (Genroku 13, 12th month; early 1701 in the Western calendar), the editor adds a small note: "Calling him Yukimura is wrong." The Sanada family's draft genealogy files his entry under "Yukimura," and a memo of drafted answers from 1809 says it was his name after he joined Osaka, yet also says no book records the change of name; the Kansei Chōshū Shokafu (per the Dai Nihon Shiryō editor's note) reads "Yukimura, first named Nobushige." In Meiji 44 (1911), Tatsukawa Bunko published Chibō Sanada Yukimura, priced at 25 sen.

Conclusion: no document from his own time found so far says "Yukimura"; who first gave him that name, and why, is still unknown.

The letters are quoted from the Dai Nihon Shiryō transcriptions, not the originals; we did not open the original Sappan Kyūki, an Edo-period copy of the Naniwa Senki, the Kansei Chōshū Shokafu, the date of the Nagasawa Kikigaki, or researchers' books, and the points on forgeries and citations rest only on Japanese Wikipedia (secondhand). Narration dates follow the old lunar calendar; sentences beginning "I think" or "we think" are this channel's view; sources are in the references below.

Illustrations are AI-generated; historical figures are unnamed cartoon characters, not likenesses; modern researchers and battles are not depicted.

Data as of 2026-10-20 (rewritten 2026-10-25 under new rules)

chapters.open-you: Taishō 6: a letter printed as a plate
chapters.genealogy: Bunka 6: asked for his original name

sv101.text: You've heard of Sanada Yukimura: the finest warrior in Japan, in games and TV dramas.

sv102.text: But who coined "Yukimura," and what year it started, no record in 300 years can say for sure.

sv103.text: In Taishō 6, Tokyo Imperial University put out a source collection printing a letter three feet long.

sv104.text: The plate's title reads: Letter of Sanada Yukimura.

sv105.text: But at the end of the letter, the writer signed: Nobushige.

sv106.text: The title and the signature differ by a name.

sv108.text: In the report with "the finest warrior in Japan," a later hand added two small characters by his name.

sv109.text: In Bunka 6 the shogunate asked, and the Sanadas drafted an answer.

sv110.text: This file goes from four letters he signed himself to that plate.

sv111.text: Did this man ever call himself "Yukimura"?

sv201.text: Sanada Nobushige is the Sanada Yukimura we all know; to learn what he called himself, read his letters.

sv202.text: The plate's letter: 3rd month, 19th day, in Osaka Castle.

sv203.text: It went to his brother-in-law, Oyamada Shigemasa, and Shigemasa's son.

sv204.text: Life is fleeting; no one knows what tomorrow brings.

sv205.text: Please no longer count me among the living.

sv206.text: Get this letter, and you'd probably not check the signature first.

sv207.text: When I first read this, I truly paused; but the signature is exactly what we're here to look at.

sv208.text: Before "Nobushige": the first character of Sanada, then his court title, Saemon-no-suke.

sv209.text: Last, a kaō: a signature drawn as a design.

sv211.text: Muramatsu, generally thought his older sister, got one opening: "Someone's going your way, so a note."

sv212.text: Of this letter's body, we read only that opening line; so why say "generally thought"?

sv213.text: Because whether she was his older or younger sister, even Edo genealogies disagree.

sv214.text: At the end he signed only his title, Saemon-no-suke,

sv215.text: written in kana, sound by sound, like talking to family.

sv216.text: But that's not the heaviest one. 2nd month, 10th day, readying for siege, he wrote to Ishiai Jūzō:

sv217.text: Holding the castle, I've resolved to die; in this life we likely won't meet again.

sv218.text: Signed: Sanada's first character, plus Saemon-no-suke.

sv219.text: All in the first 3 months of one year.

sv220.text: And earlier, how did he sign?

sv221.text: In his years at Kudoyama, he wrote someone asking for liquor:

sv222.text: Please fill this jar with shōchū and send it.

sv223.text: It went to someone named Sakyō; no year is given, and it's signed "Kōhaku, Nobushige."

sv225.text: Not two months after the plate's letter, on Keichō 20, 5th month, 7th day, he fell at Osaka.

sv226.text: Researchers note: the day before he died, his citations for six retainers were on small shogi-like wood pieces;

sv228.text: So much for the name in his own hand; what did others call him?

sv301.text: Enemies wrote of him too. 5th month, 15th day: daimyo Hosokawa Tadaoki, writing home, called him "Sanada Saemon-no-suke,"

sv302.text: and said his feat was unmatched, past or present.

sv303.text: In a letter four days earlier, he paired Sanada's and Gotō Matabei's units: also unmatched.

sv304.text: Surprisingly, the most famous line isn't in an enemy letter: a Shimazu postwar report also wrote of him.

sv305.text: The report is dated Keichō 20, 6th month, 11th day: just over a month after his death.

sv306.text: So the battle had just ended; news was still en route.

sv307.text: What we read is the print in that Taishō 6 collection: its opening is missing, and it ends unsigned.

sv309.text: It's in lord Shimazu Iehisa's family records;

sv310.text: But that doesn't mean Iehisa wrote it; the paper leaves no writer's name.

sv311.text: Later historians could only say: news a Shimazu samurai sent from Kamigata home to Satsuma.

sv312.text: That opening phrase, "the finest warrior in Japan," is in this report:

sv313.text: Sanada is the finest warrior in Japan, unmatched even in tales of old.

sv314.text: It ends with "yoshi," meaning: so they say.

sv315.text: It says it's all anyone talks of;

sv316.text: So is this praise the writer's own view?

sv317.text: No; the report closes by stating these were noted from rumors among the men.

sv318.text: The writer left an out: if anything's off, he'll report again.

sv319.text: See "I heard" in a group chat and you'd probably take it with a grain of salt; that's how I felt here.

sv320.text: What does the report call him?

sv321.text: His title again: throughout, he's "Sanada Saemon," or simply "Sanada."

sv322.text: But the print has two tiny characters by "Sanada Saemon":

sv324.text: That's the later addition from the start; the report's own words lack it.

sv325.text: Unclear who added it; most likely it came when the report was copied.

sv326.text: That's odd: the writer never used the name, yet someone felt it had to be added.

sv327.text: So what book first put "Yukimura" in writing?

sv401.text: Generally thought the first: an Osaka war chronicle, the Naniwa Senki.

sv402.text: Its preface was written in Kanbun 12, 57 years after the Osaka battles.

sv403.text: 57 years: roughly from your grandpa's birth to you growing up, right?

sv404.text: It says: second son of Sanada Masayuki, lord of Ueda Castle, Saemon-no-suke Yukimura.

sv405.text: His grandfather Yukitaka, father Masayuki and son Yukimasa all share the character "yuki";

sv406.text: But the book says not a word on why "Yukimura."

sv407.text: You may think: so "what year it started" is the preface's year?

sv409.text: We can't say that yet. That preface was written for the two original authors.

sv410.text: What we read: a later, expanded copy.

sv411.text: What year did the expander get to work?

sv412.text: He gave no year; only that he split it into ten volumes and gave it a new title.

sv413.text: In the Shōwa 3 reprint, the editor wrote: all inverted sentences were redone in mixed kana, and wording was revised.

sv414.text: We can't tell if the original had "Yukimura."

sv415.text: So is there a record we can actually date?

sv416.text: Yes. In Genroku 13, 12th month, Tokugawa Mitsukuni of Mito died; by the Western calendar, already early 1701.

sv417.text: After his death, Mito domain men compiled his words and deeds, the Tōgen Iji, from notes kept by his physician.

sv418.text: It records Mitsukuni speaking of Sanada, calling him "Nobuyori." Here's the catch:

sv419.text: Right under that name, the editor added a note in small script:

sv421.text: That's the editor speaking, not Mitsukuni.

sv422.text: You can tell that by then "Yukimura" had spread enough to need a correction.

sv423.text: Did you notice? Even "Calling him Yukimura is wrong" is written small, off to the side.

sv424.text: But does their "Nobuyori" match his letters?

sv425.text: No; "Nobuyori" appears nowhere in his letters.

sv426.text: The later Okinagusa essays retold it as Mitsukuni's own research rejecting "Yukimura."

sv427.text: It adds it can't say how to read the second character.

sv428.text: We think even "who said Yukimura was wrong" got rewritten by later hands.

sv429.text: Outsiders called "Yukimura" wrong; how did the Sanadas record him?

sv501.text: The Sanada family's later draft genealogy titles his entry "Yukimura."

sv502.text: Under it: as a child, Benmaru, also Genjirō; born Eiroku 10, aged 49 the year he went to Osaka.

sv504.text: The draft says: first named Nobushige; at Mount Kōya, he went by Kōhaku.

sv505.text: That opening question came in Bunka 6, 11th month: a shogunate inspector asked about the old Sanada tree.

sv506.text: One question: was Nobushige his original name?

sv507.text: You're a Sanada retainer, asked an ancestor's name from nearly 200 years ago. Your answer?

sv508.text: The Sanadas drafted a memo of how to answer: yes, Nobushige was his original name.

sv509.text: The memo also notes that an earlier filing gave both names, Nobushige and Yukimura.

sv511.text: The drafted reply: a name used only after he left the Sanadas and joined the Osaka side;

sv513.text: This is only a memo; we haven't seen what was actually sent.

sv514.text: Remember the three Keichō 20 letters from Osaka Castle?

sv515.text: Said to be his name only after Osaka, yet those three letters are signed Nobushige or Saemon-no-suke.

sv519.text: His renaming to Yukimura appears in no book at all.

sv520.text: Is there any letter he signed "Yukimura"?

sv521.text: Two copies survive, no originals; researchers judge both to be forgeries.

sv522.text: Not just the Sanadas: per the collection's editor, the shogunate's official Kansei Chōshū Shokafu also reads "Yukimura, first named Nobushige."

sv523.text: How did a name with no source even in his own family become known nationwide?

sv602.text: In Meiji 44, nearly 300 years after his death, Tatsukawa Bunko published No. 5: Chibō Sanada Yukimura.

sv603.text: Priced at 25 sen; in the same ad, volume 1 was Ikkyū Zenji.

sv604.text: I think choosing him in a game is the same as Meiji readers paying 25 sen:

sv606.text: And so "Sanada Yukimura" became a name known nationwide.

sv607.text: Still no one could say where the name came from, but it had already run ahead.

sv609.text: Its contents list says "Sanada Yukimura, general of Osaka";

sv610.text: Even the shōchū letter's margin heading says: Yukimura wants shōchū.

sv611.text: The Shimazu report is a day off; a note fixes it. Guess what it calls him?

sv613.text: Even annotating Muramatsu's letter, the editor wrote "Yukimura's older sister."

sv615.text: Not just this book: a kaō collection traced his signature, titled "Sanada Yukimura"; the tracing still reads "Nobushige."

sv616.text: Traced from another letter to the Ishiai family.

sv617.text: We think that plate's title records exactly what that era called him.

sv618.text: So, the opening question: did he ever call himself "Yukimura"?

sv619.text: The opening point still holds after these records: who first used it, and why, we don't know;

sv620.text: But whether he used it himself, the records can answer.

sv621.text: Of the documents from his time found so far, not one says "Yukimura." This file: archived.

sv623.text: Where did you first hear "Sanada Yukimura": a game, a TV drama, or a book? Tell me below.

sv624.text: This channel tells only what records hold; subscribe to open files with us.
